items.headline: Now Microsoft Defender can discover the AI agents running on company laptops
items.explanation: On October 19, 2026 Microsoft announced it is extending Project Perception to secure 'the agentic insider': Guardian Agents watch AI agents and contain risky actions, and Microsoft Defender can now discover dozens of local AI agent types (such as coding agents) once it sees them running on onboarded devices. The message is that agents need their own identity, least-privilege permissions and monitoring, just like people.
items.why: AI agents are becoming a new kind of identity. Companies will need IAM people who can give agents their own identities, scope their access, review it and remove it, which is JML for agents. Saying this in an interview shows you're current.
items.say: Did you know Microsoft now treats AI agents as insiders that need their own identity and least-privilege access?
items.source_label: Microsoft Security Blog: Agents are your newest insiders (Oct 19, 2026)

items.headline: A remote-access tool used by IT admins had a zero-day that attackers exploited
items.explanation: BeyondTrust Remote Support (formerly Bomgar) had a critical flaw, CVE-2026-102764, that let an unauthenticated attacker run file operations on the appliance. A suspected China-linked espionage group exploited it in late August 2026. CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list on October 16 and urged everyone to patch right away.
items.why: BeyondTrust is a privileged access (PAM) vendor. Remote support tools hold the keys to many machines, so they are prime targets. IAM and PAM teams have to patch them fast, limit who can reach their admin pages, and rotate credentials after an incident.
items.say: When a privileged-access tool like BeyondTrust has a zero-day, I'd patch it, restrict admin access to trusted networks, review the logs, and rotate any credentials it stored.

items.headline: Browsers blocked 8 eMudhra certificate authorities after their keys turned out to be weak
items.explanation: The private keys for eight eMudhra intermediate certificate authorities were generated with too little randomness, so anyone could forge HTTPS certificates. Chrome, Firefox, Apple and Microsoft blocked them within days, and Chrome is removing the related root on October 27.
items.why: Certificates are identities for machines and websites. This is a reminder that 'non-human identity' includes certificates, and they need inventory, rotation, and fast revocation, just like user accounts.
items.say: Certificates are machine identities. The eMudhra incident shows why you need a certificate inventory and a way to replace them quickly.

items.headline: DHS ordered federal agencies to remove DeepSeek AI products
items.explanation: A DHS order made public October 20 requires federal civilian agencies to remove DeepSeek products, including third-party tools built on DeepSeek models, and stop buying them. DHS cited data going to servers in China and app vulnerabilities.
items.why: Companies are writing similar 'approved AI tools' policies. Controlling which apps people can sign into (app governance, Conditional Access, blocking unsanctioned SaaS) is IAM work.
items.say: Banning an AI tool only works if identity controls back it up, for example blocking sign-in to unapproved apps with Conditional Access.

items.headline: Shared AI chats from Meta Muse were findable by anyone through DNS records
items.explanation: Researchers at Claroc found more than 6,800 shared Muse conversation links in passive DNS. The chat title was built into the web address, and the pages opened without a login. Some held loan applications and confidential business notes. Meta paused the sharing feature.
items.why: 'Anyone with the link' is not access control. Good IAM means sharing tied to a named identity, with expiry and review, which is the same idea behind access reviews in Entra.
items.say: The Muse leak is a good example of why 'anyone with the link' sharing is risky. Access should be tied to an identity and expire.
